items.why: The answer is explicit, but the broad negative question permits many possible responses.
Awkward pronouns blur whether the message comes from the man of God, the prophet, or the Lord.
The closing summary clearly credits David and his men rather than Jonathan alone.
The officer is the clear referent of the trampling account, not the man of God.
The sons saddle the donkey, but the old prophet explicitly mounts it.
The passage explicitly contrasts the first three-party covenant with the second covenant.
Jotham’s succession is the clearly stated event following Uzziah’s burial.
The passage explicitly says Uzziah was eager to leave because the Lord afflicted him.
The quoted plan clearly ends with entering the city, though the question is stiffly phrased.
Their decision to surrender at the Aramean camp is explicit and contrasts with entering the city.
Sibbekai appears in the first battle report, though “who kills first” is slightly unnatural.
The answer “the news” fails to state what information was reported.
Jeroboam’s command to seize the man of God is direct and unambiguous.
Uzziah is explicitly the person whom Azariah and the priests follow inside.
The chronology supports tomorrow, but “the other woman” is perspective-dependent.
Zechariah is directly identified as Uzziah’s instructor in fearing God.
Elisha’s reply to the officer’s doubt is clearly distinguished from his earlier price prophecy.
The man of God explicitly grounds his refusal in the Lord’s command.
Talking until daylight is the last stated action before Paul leaves.
Mobilizing the army clearly precedes marching to and besieging Samaria.
Jehoiada gives the weapons, while David is only identified as their former owner.
The accusers are explicitly ordered to present their case to the letter’s addressee.
The people’s stated purpose is to make Uzziah king in Amaziah’s place.
The 307,500 soldiers are explicitly under the command of the 2,600 family leaders.
The traveler killed by the lion is clearly the man of God, not the prophet.
This duplicates Q89C41’s officer-trampling event without adding a distinct concept.
The instructions clearly assign the two off-duty companies to guard the temple for the king.
The letter heading plainly distinguishes Claudius Lysias as writer from Felix as recipient.
Abishai directly kills Ishbi-Benob while rescuing David.
After admitting wrongdoing, the men explicitly resolve to report immediately to the palace.
Paul directly says that the young man has something to tell the commander.
The messengers’ return and report immediately precede the camp’s plundering.
Uzziah is the clear antecedent, but the wording about explaining farm work is contrived.
The woman explicitly says that her own son was cooked and eaten first.
The man of God explicitly intercedes after the king requests prayer.
The passage gives a complete three-group list and separates the tribute-paying Ammonites.
The prophet first brings the body to his city and only afterward places it in his tomb.
Joash is clearly identified as the child hidden with his nurse for six years.
The text explicitly attributes the city’s calm to Athaliah’s death at the palace.
The two centurions receive the order; the soldiers are part of the detachment to prepare.
The Arameans explicitly believe the Hittite and Egyptian kings are coming to attack.
The murderer is the king who sends the messenger, not the messenger himself.
In the old prophet’s claimed message, the man of God is the person to be brought back to eat.
Paul’s intention to leave the next day is explicitly linked to his prolonged speaking.
The passage directly contrasts the cavalry continuing with the soldiers returning.
The plural victims who flee are the seven sons whom the possessed man beat.
The vague phrase “items’ arrival” makes a straightforward healing event obscure.
The conspirators explicitly ask the council to have the commander bring Paul.
Replacing the clearly named scrolls with vague “materials” makes the sequence needlessly obscure.
The quoted order specifically condemns anyone who follows the woman, not the woman herself.
Athaliah hears the noise before going to the people and sees the king only afterward.
The conspirators are explicitly waiting for the commander’s consent, though “act” is vague.
The warning is directly addressed to the man of God from Judah, not the old prophet.
The prophecy names Josiah as the person who will sacrifice the high-place priests.
